when: a GPU-side operation that can run while device memory or the KV pool is nearly full allocates temporaries whose size scales with the request or data size
expect: Ask the author to report the peak extra device memory for a long request. If it is unbounded or large, ask them to process the work in chunks with a fixed byte cap. Any ordering guarantee the unchunked version relied on must still hold across chunk boundaries, and a test must verify the chunked result matches the unchunked one.
why: Temporaries proportional to request size can OOM exactly when memory is scarcest, and naive chunking can break overlap or ordering assumptions.
examples: KV compaction or block-move gather allocating a buffer sized to a 128K-token request; chunk under a byte cap and ensure earlier destinations never overwrite later sources
a gather kernel that materializes all selected blocks at once instead of in capped batches
concern: Bound GPU temporary memory in KV operations under pool pressure (chunk with byte cap, preserve ordering)

when: code writes in place into paged KV cache blocks owned by the serving engine
expect: Ask for exclusive block ownership to be documented as an explicit precondition of the writing function. Check that every caller guarantees the blocks are private before writing, either by copy-on-write or by excluding those requests from prefix caching.
why: With prefix caching, the engine may share one physical KV block among several requests, so an in-place write silently corrupts other requests' KV.
examples: a function that compacts or relocates KV inside vLLM paged blocks without checking whether a block is shared via the prefix cache
concern: In-place writes to paged KV blocks must ensure exclusive ownership (prefix-cache sharing)

when: a change alters LMCache behavior to compensate for how an upstream engine reports or handles state
expect: Ask the PR description to state the upstream semantics being relied on, including what the engine is expected to report and why the observed behavior deviates from it. It must also justify why the fix belongs in LMCache rather than upstream, or link an upstream issue or PR.
why: Undocumented workarounds encode assumptions about upstream behavior that break silently when upstream changes, and they may hide an upstream bug.
examples: filtering load-only requests out of vLLM's finished_sending, where only requests that performed a store should appear
concern: Justify vLLM-semantics workarounds in LMCache and why not fixed upstream

when: a docstring explains in prose a multi-step or non-obvious state transformation that the reader has to simulate in their head
expect: Ask for a self-contained worked example in the docstring that shows the initial state, the arguments of successive calls, and the resulting state after each call.
why: Prose alone for stateful transformations is ambiguous and hard to verify, while a concrete trace makes both intent and bugs visible.
examples: a function tracking block ids under speculative relocation, documented only in prose
concern: Docstrings for non-obvious state changes need a worked example

when: a reconnection or recovery path restores a connection to a peer that negotiated parameters during the initial handshake
expect: Check that recovery re-runs the full handshake negotiation, not just resource re-registration. It must verify every renegotiated parameter against the values the local side cached, and only then mark the connection healthy or re-register resources. Mismatches must be handled explicitly.
why: A restarted peer comes back with its configured defaults while the local side still holds previously negotiated values, which leads to silent inconsistency.
examples: vLLM multiprocess adapter reconnecting to a restarted LMCache server that only re-registers KV and never renegotiates chunk size
concern: Recovery/reconnect must re-run handshake negotiation and verify before marking healthy

when: a change adds behavior specific to one accelerator vendor, device type or platform inside shared, device-agnostic code, by any form of special-casing: a conditional on device/backend identity, a special-cased helper, a vendor-only code path or fallback, or a vendor-specific module or API wired directly into the generic layer
expect: ask the author to remove the device/vendor check from the shared code and move the vendor-specific behavior behind the existing device/platform abstraction (backend interface, registry or plugin that each accelerator implements), so the generic code calls one uniform API; if that abstraction lacks the needed operation, extend the interface rather than branching on device kind in the shared layer. A new accelerator should be addable without editing the generic code
why: each per-device special case in shared code is effectively a vendor fork that later changes must maintain, that grows with every new accelerator, and that makes generic logic depend on hardware details
examples: `if device_type == "musa"` branches in multiprocess/transfer code for event record, stream wait and IPC handle export; instead route these through a device backend method that MUSA and CUDA each implement
a generic transfer path that imports or calls vendor-specific stream/event APIs directly, or adds a vendor-only fallback, rather than going through a per-device backend implementation
concern: no device/vendor-specific branching in generic code; use a device backend abstraction

when: A change makes shared, generic code depend on specific optional or experimental features, pluggable implementations or accelerator vendors/devices, so adding, removing or plugging in one requires editing shared or existing code. Shared code here means anything meant to serve all of them, such as an integration layer, coordinator, API layer, transfer path, registry or dispatcher. Typical forms: importing or looking up a specific class or module; holding state named after it; branching on its presence or on its identity, including a growing conditional chain over a kind discriminator (engine, format, vendor, device); adding a special-cased helper, code path or fallback for it; inlining its logic or documentation into a shared hook or handler, including a hook that is a no-op on the core path; or keeping many interchangeable implementations together in one file behind a hand-maintained registry.
expect: Ask the author to move each specific behavior and its documentation into its own module or package, one per implementation. The shared layer should reach them only through one generic extension point. Acceptable forms are: (a) a dispatcher created once at init, with each lifecycle hook forwarding to it by one generic call that names the hook and passes the hook's arguments; (b) a strategy or registration mechanism, where each implementation registers itself or is discovered by scanning its package, and the shared code selects one by key instead of through a conditional chain; or (c) the existing device/platform backend interface that each accelerator implements, extended with the missing operation if needed rather than branched around. The shared layer must hold no names, imports, lookups, presence or identity checks, conditional chains or inlined logic for any specific feature, implementation or vendor. Adding, removing or plugging in an out-of-tree implementation must need no edit to existing files.
why: Hardcoding specific implementations in shared code couples the core to every feature, grows files without bound and turns each addition into an edit to shared code that risks merge conflicts.
examples: vLLM connector added `self.<feature>` plus `if self.<feature> is not None:` blocks in `register_kv_caches`/`wait_for_save`. Reviewer asked for `self.dispatcher = init_dispatcher(kwargs)` from `lmcache.experimental.engine_side` in `__init__` and `self.dispatcher.dispatch("register_kv_caches", **kwargs)` in the hook.

MP connector's no-op `save_kv_layer` was filled with an experimental feature's logic and docstring. Reviewer asked for `self.dispatcher.dispatch("save_kv_layer", **kwargs)` with the behavior documented in the experimental module.

`if device_type == "musa"` branches in multiprocess/transfer code for event record, stream wait and IPC handle export. These should go through a device backend method that MUSA and CUDA each implement.
A generic transfer path imports or calls vendor-specific stream/event APIs directly, or adds a vendor-only fallback, instead of going through a per-device backend implementation.

The MP coordinator's shared HTTP API layer called `ctx.controllers.get(FleetEvictionController)` to serve that controller's endpoints. Controllers can be out-of-tree, so the reviewer asked that each controller package register its own HTTP routes instead of the shared layer hardcoding which controllers exist.

All spec implementations lived in one large file with manual registration, causing growth and merge conflicts. Reviewer asked for one file per spec in a package, loaded by dynamic scanning, so a new spec changes no existing line.
An `if/elif` chain on engine type selected the format detection logic. Reviewer asked for a strategy pattern: a set of per-engine format detector objects selected by key.
concern: keep experimental features out of the connector; route all hooks through one generic dispatcher

when: a change in the multiprocess server adds a request handler, changes which dispatch mode a handler uses, makes an existing SYNC handler do more or slower work, or touches the liveness/health-check path
expect: SYNC handlers all run on the single server-side dispatcher thread, so any slow SYNC handler stalls every other SYNC handler. Before accepting a handler on SYNC, the author must show it cannot run long or block (heavy setup or registration, I/O, locks, waiting on other components). Otherwise, move it to BLOCKING dispatch on the shared worker pool. Do not put liveness/health handlers on SYNC while any SYNC handler can block. Put them on BLOCKING dispatch on the shared worker pool, so a timeout reflects real pool saturation, or on a dedicated responder thread. Flag any new long-running handler placed on SYNC.
why: A liveness probe queued behind a slow handler on the dispatcher thread reports a healthy server as dead. That pushes vLLM into degraded/downgrade mode for the wrong reason. When the probe shares the worker pool, its timeout does signal real saturation, which is when downgrade is appropriate.
examples: A PR moved PING to SYNC dispatch while REGISTER_KV_CACHE was also SYNC and can occupy the dispatcher thread for a while. The reviewer asked to put PING on BLOCKING with the normal thread pool for now.
Long-term plan from the same review: move REGISTER_KV_CACHE to BLOCKING dispatch and give PING its own responder thread.
concern: Keep liveness/PING handlers off the single SYNC dispatcher thread; check whether a handler can block it before choosing SYNC

when: a change adds or modifies an MP engine submodule, makes one submodule use state or functionality owned by another submodule, or a design doc describes how MP engine submodules collaborate
expect: The MP engine is an ownership tree. The engine context owns the storage manager and every submodule, and each submodule holds a reference only to the context. Flag any sibling reference, however it is made: constructor injection, a setter, a stored attribute, or a lookup that reaches into another submodule's internals. Require the cross-submodule call to go through a context method that dispatches to the owning submodule, and add that method if it does not exist yet. Ask that design docs describe the same ownership-and-dispatch structure.
why: Direct sibling links break the single-owner tree. They create hidden coupling and lifecycle and ordering dependencies between submodules, and they bypass the context as the one dispatch point.
examples: ManagementModule (answers PING) needed to touch or reap instances tracked by the GPU/CPU transfer modules. The reviewer asked it to call `self._ctx.<method>` and let MPEngineContext dispatch, instead of receiving the transfer modules by injection.
BlendV3Module and the GPU/CPU transfer modules are siblings under MPEngineContext, so none of them should hold a reference to another.
concern: MP engine ownership tree: submodules reference only the context and reach siblings via context dispatch, never direct sibling wiring

tests.note: same reviewer (ApostaC) as the evidence; human severity minor

when: a change puts a capability (method, abstract hook or attribute) on a base class or shared base type because every current subclass happens to need it, although the capability is not inherent to what that base type represents or could also apply to classes outside that hierarchy
expect: Ask the author to justify that every future subclass must have the capability and that no class outside the hierarchy will ever need it; if they cannot, move it into a separate opt-in interface, mixin or protocol that any class can implement, and have callers depend on that interface rather than on the base type.
why: Putting an incidental capability on a base type couples the base to an unrelated concern, forces it on future subclasses that may not need it, and excludes classes outside the hierarchy that could.
examples: `get_durable_components` was added as a method of `View` only because all existing Views implement it; the reviewer asked whether every future View will have it and whether a non-View class never will, pointing toward a separate interface/mixin.
concern: Model optional capabilities as opt-in interfaces/mixins, not base-class methods

tests.note: base holds a field only some subclasses use; AI suggested the opposite (hoist caching into base)

when: a change creates, records, passes or waits on a GPU synchronization event for a KV transfer between LMCache and the serving engine, or merges event creation for different transfer paths into one shared path
expect: Check that the event type is chosen by who drives the transfer. Transfers that LMCache drives across process boundaries need an interprocess (IPC) event. Transfers that the engine drives need a normal local event. An async engine-driven transfer must still create and keep a local event for synchronization and must never pass None. Reject a single event-creation path that ignores the transfer context, and ask the author to select the event type explicitly for each transfer context.
why: A local event cannot be waited on from another process. An IPC event adds needless overhead on engine-driven paths. An async transfer that passes no event loses its synchronization, so the consumer can read KV data before the copy finishes.
examples: The reviewer asked that event creation select the type from the actual transfer context. LMCache-driven transfers get an IPC event, and engine-driven transfers get a normal local event. Async engine-driven transfers keep a local event rather than passing None.
concern: GPU event type must match who drives the transfer (IPC vs local, never None for async)

when: code that can fall back at runtime to another copy or version of a component it depends on (a vendored, bundled, older or third-party implementation) is changed to call a method or attribute that only the primary or newer copy provides
expect: Every API the changed code calls must exist on every implementation the fallback can select. If one does not, ask the author for one of three fixes. They can add a compatibility helper that feature-detects the API and keeps the previous behavior when it is missing. They can remove the fallback. Or they can sync the API into the other copy. Require the same fix at every call site that uses the new API and in every version-specific variant of the caller, not just the one in the diff.
why: Local tests use the primary implementation, so they pass. In deployments that select the other copy, the fallback path raises AttributeError at request time instead.
examples: A connector still fell back to vLLM's vendored LMCacheMPWorkerAdapter. The PR moved event creation, which the connector used to do inline, into a new `create_and_record_event` method that exists only on the LMCache-owned adapter. The fix had to cover both the load and store paths and every version-specific connector variant.
concern: Connector fallback to vendored adapter may only call APIs present in the vendored version

when: a change makes any object other than the single owner that is cleared on engine disconnect retain a reference to the serving engine's GPU KV cache tensors, or to views, wrappers or containers of them, beyond a single call. This covers an attribute on a helper, descriptor, adapter or spec, a cache or registry entry, a closure, and module-level state.
expect: Ask the author to pass the engine KV tensors into each call that needs them, or to keep them only in the single owner whose state is cleared on engine disconnect. For any new holder that must retain such a reference, ask the author to show in the diff where the disconnect or teardown path releases it. No second holder may outlive the owner.
why: Every reference to the engine's GPU KV tensors must be dropped when the serving engine disconnects. A stray long-lived reference pins GPU memory after disconnect and leaks it.
examples: A KVFormatSpec object stored the raw `kv_caches` list as an attribute. The reviewer flagged the memory-leak risk and asked that all references to the GPU KV tensors be removable when the serving engine disconnects.
concern: Do not hold long-lived references to engine GPU KV tensors; they must be droppable on disconnect

when: a change adds, refactors or touches code that is used only by the legacy non-MP (non-multiprocess) mode, or adds or modifies a base class or interface whose methods are split between MP-mode use and non-MP-only use
expect: Ask the author to mark non-MP-only code paths with the project's deprecation annotation so they emit a deprecation warning. For base classes and interfaces, ask them to document per method whether MP mode requires it or only legacy non-MP mode uses it. Legacy-only code must not be left silently maintained without a marker.
why: Non-MP mode is legacy and slated for removal. Its code must be identifiable so that implementers know what is actually required and later cleanups know what to delete.
examples: A function used only by non-MP mode was refactored without any warning. The reviewer asked for the `lmcache_deprecate` annotation on it.
A base class defined many methods with no indication of which ones MP mode uses. The reviewer asked the author to clarify which are used in MP mode and which are used only in non-MP mode.
concern: Explicitly mark legacy non-MP-only code (deprecation annotation or documentation) so it is identifiable for removal

when: A change adds or keeps logic in an orchestrating/driver module that builds, derives inputs for, or reads into the internals of a data structure owned by another module, such as a descriptor, plan or spec that the driver hands to another component. This includes exposing that structure's sub-builders or internal types as public functions, and changes where adding a field or parameter to the structure forces edits in the driver.
expect: Ask the author to move the construction and derivation helpers into the module that owns the structure. That module should expose a minimal public API, ideally one entry point to build the structure from the driver's context and one to consume it. Its sub-builders, helpers and intermediate types should stay private, and the driver should call only those entry points. Ask the author to confirm that adding a new parameter or field to the structure would change only the owning module and leave the driver untouched.
why: If the driver knows a structure's internals, every change to the driver/structure contract ripples into the driver. A narrow build/consume API keeps the driver thin and confines future contract changes to the owning module.
examples: lmcache_driven_transfer.py defined public functions that derived layout metadata from the cache context and built per-kernel-group and per-object-group transfer descriptors. The reviewer asked to move them into the descriptor/plan module behind one build function and one consume function each, so that a new kernel-group or object-group parameter would not require edits to the driver.

The top-level 'cache context -> resolved transfer descriptor' builder was moved into the descriptor module. To avoid an import cycle, that module uses duck typing and imports the cache-context class only under TYPE_CHECKING.
concern: Transfer descriptor/plan building lives in the descriptor module behind a minimal public API; the driver stays thin
